name: Wolfram syndrome
aliases: diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy and deafness

reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Usually autosomal recessive neurodegenerative and endocrine disorder caused by WFS1 mutations encoding wolframin, an endoplasmic reticulum membrane protein; a rarer CISD2-related form exists
The acronym DIDMOAD summarises the core features: Diabetes Insipidus, Diabetes Mellitus, Optic Atrophy, and Deafness
Childhood-onset non-autoimmune, insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus is typically the first feature, followed by progressive bilateral optic atrophy causing visual loss
The diabetes mellitus is islet-cell-antibody negative and not HLA-associated, distinguishing it from type 1 diabetes, and coexisting optic atrophy should prompt consideration of Wolfram syndrome
Cranial diabetes insipidus, sensorineural deafness, neurodegeneration (brainstem and cerebellar signs, neurogenic bladder), and psychiatric disturbance develop over time
Diagnosis is clinical supported by WFS1 sequencing; management is supportive and multidisciplinary, coordinating diabetes, endocrine, ophthalmology, audiology, urology, and neurology care
reference.pathophysiology: Wolfram syndrome is most often caused by biallelic WFS1 mutations encoding wolframin, an endoplasmic reticulum transmembrane protein important for calcium homeostasis and the endoplasmic reticulum stress response. Loss of wolframin function heightens endoplasmic reticulum stress and triggers apoptosis in highly secretory and neuronal cells, notably pancreatic beta cells, retinal ganglion cells and the optic nerve, the hypothalamic-pituitary vasopressin system, the cochlea, and diffuse brain regions. This progressive cellular loss produces non-autoimmune insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy, cranial diabetes insipidus, sensorineural deafness, and wider neurodegeneration.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated hereditary optic atrophy (e.g. dominant optic atrophy, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy)
Mitochondrial disease with diabetes and deafness (e.g. maternally inherited diabetes and deafness)
Other causes of cranial diabetes insipidus
Thiamine-responsive megaloblastic anaemia syndrome (SLC19A2) with diabetes and deafness
Bardet-Biedl and other syndromic causes of visual and endocrine disturbance
additionalInvestigations: WFS1 (and CISD2) gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis
Diabetes work-up including islet autoantibodies (negative) and C-peptide
Water deprivation/desmopressin testing and paired plasma/urine osmolality for diabetes insipidus
Formal ophthalmological assessment with optical coherence tomography and visual fields for optic atrophy
Brain MRI to assess brainstem, cerebellar, and posterior pituitary changes; urodynamics for neurogenic bladder
redFlags: Progressive visual loss from optic atrophy threatening independence
Unrecognised cranial diabetes insipidus causing dehydration and electrolyte disturbance
Brainstem neurodegeneration with central apnoea or swallowing difficulty
Severe psychiatric disturbance or suicidality requiring urgent mental-health support
reference.prognosis: Wolfram syndrome is progressive with accumulating disability; visual and hearing loss, neurological decline, and endocrine complications develop over years, and premature death, often from brainstem involvement or its complications, is typical. Coordinated multidisciplinary care can preserve function and quality of life.
pitfalls: Labelling the childhood diabetes as type 1 and missing the syndromic diagnosis when optic atrophy appears
Attributing polyuria solely to poor glycaemic control and overlooking coexisting cranial diabetes insipidus
Neglecting audiological, urological, and psychiatric surveillance in a multisystem disorder
Failing to offer genetic counselling given the mainly autosomal recessive inheritance
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists, so care is supportive and directed at the DIDMOAD components
Insulin replacement for the non-autoimmune, insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus that is usually the first feature
Desmopressin replacement for cranial diabetes insipidus
Low-vision support and ophthalmology follow-up for progressive optic atrophy, and hearing aids or cochlear implantation for sensorineural deafness
Management of neurogenic bladder with intermittent catheterisation and anticholinergic agents, alongside neurological and psychiatric symptomatic care
Coordinated multidisciplinary surveillance spanning endocrinology, ophthalmology, audiology, urology, neurology and psychiatry given the progressive course
Genetic counselling for this usually autosomal recessive WFS1-related disorder, with family testing
